P1● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

How many covalent bonds are there in a molecule of butane, CX4HX10\ce{C4H10}CX4​HX10​?

every line in a structural formula is one covalent bond (Topics 1–3).

10 counts only the C–H bonds.
A chain of 4 carbons has 3 C–C bonds; there are 10 C–H bonds; 3 + 10 = 13.
14 is the number of atoms, not bonds.
4 is the number of carbon atoms.

Asked: the total number of covalent bonds in butane.

Concept used: every line in a structural formula is one covalent bond (Topics 1–3).

  1. Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✘ 10 counts only the C–H bonds.
    • (b) ✔ A chain of 4 carbons has 3 C–C bonds; there are 10 C–H bonds; 3 + 10 = 13.
    • (c) ✘ 14 is the number of atoms, not bonds.
    • (d) ✘ 4 is the number of carbon atoms.

  2. Answer (b)

P2● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

In which molecule do the two atoms share three pairs of electrons?

atoms share as many pairs as they need electrons: N needs 3, O 2, Cl 1, H 1 (Topic 2).

Each O needs 2 → two shared pairs (double bond).
Each N (2, 5) needs 3 → three shared pairs.
Each Cl needs 1 → one shared pair.
Each H needs 1 → one shared pair.

Asked: the molecule with a triple bond.

Concept used: atoms share as many pairs as they need electrons: N needs 3, O 2, Cl 1, H 1 (Topic 2).

  1. Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✘ Each O needs 2 → two shared pairs (double bond).
    • (b) ✔ Each N (2, 5) needs 3 → three shared pairs.
    • (c) ✘ Each Cl needs 1 → one shared pair.
    • (d) ✘ Each H needs 1 → one shared pair.

  2. Answer (b)

P3● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

In the electron-dot structure of water, HX2O\ce{H2O}HX2​O, the oxygen atom has:

O has 6 valence electrons; it shares one pair with each H and keeps the rest as lone pairs (Topic 2).

2 shared pairs (4 electrons) + 2 lone pairs (4 electrons) = 8.
Oxygen would have only 4 electrons — the lone pairs have been forgotten.
That gives only 6 electrons round O — one lone pair is missing.
With one shared pair, only one H could be attached.

Asked: shared and lone pairs round O in water.

Concept used: O has 6 valence electrons; it shares one pair with each H and keeps the rest as lone pairs (Topic 2).

  1. Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✔ 2 shared pairs (4 electrons) + 2 lone pairs (4 electrons) = 8.
    • (b) ✘ Oxygen would have only 4 electrons — the lone pairs have been forgotten.
    • (c) ✘ That gives only 6 electrons round O — one lone pair is missing.
    • (d) ✘ With one shared pair, only one H could be attached.

  2. Answer (a)

P6● FoundationVery short answer · 2 marksOriginal

(a) Write the formula and name of the next member of the homologous series of CX2HX5OH\ce{C2H5OH}CX2​HX5​OH. (b) Write the general formula of the alkynes and the name of the first member.

Full solution

Given: CX2HX5OH\ce{C2H5OH}CX2​HX5​OH; the alkyne series. Asked: next homologue; general formula and first alkyne.

Concept used: successive members differ by CHX2\ce{CH2}CHX2​; alkynes have a C≡C\ce{C#C}C≡C bond (Topic 4).

  1. 1

    (a) Add CHX2\ce{CH2}CHX2​: CX2HX5OH\ce{C2H5OH}CX2​HX5​OH → CX3HX7OH\ce{C3H7OH}CX3​HX7​OH, propanol.

  2. 2

    (b) Alkynes: CnH2n−2\mathrm{C}_n\mathrm{H}_{2n-2}Cn​H2n−2​. A triple bond needs two carbons, so the first member has nnn = 2: CX2HX2\ce{C2H2}CX2​HX2​, ethyne.

  3. Check: CX3HX7OH\ce{C3H7OH}CX3​HX7​OH − CX2HX5OH\ce{C2H5OH}CX2​HX5​OH = CHX2\ce{CH2}CHX2​ ✔; for nnn = 2, 2 × 2 − 2 = 2 hydrogens → CX2HX2\ce{C2H2}CX2​HX2​ ✔.

  4. Answer (a) CX3HX7OH\ce{C3H7OH}CX3​HX7​OH, propanol (b) CnH2n−2\mathrm{C}_n\mathrm{H}_{2n-2}Cn​H2n−2​; ethyne, CX2HX2\ce{C2H2}CX2​HX2​

    Common trap: Giving "methyne" as the first alkyne. One carbon cannot form a triple bond.

P7● FoundationFill in the blank · 2 marksOriginal

Fill in the blanks.
(a) The ability of carbon atoms to bond with other carbon atoms to form long chains is called ________.
(b) Carbon can form bonds with four other atoms because it shows ________.
(c) Hydrocarbons with only single bonds between carbon atoms are called ________ hydrocarbons.
(d) Ethene, with a double bond, is an ________ hydrocarbon.

Full solution

Given: — Asked: the missing words.

Concept used: carbon's properties; saturated and unsaturated hydrocarbons (Topic 3).

  1. 1

    (a) catenation

  2. 2

    (b) tetravalency (a valency of four)

  3. 3

    (c) saturated

  4. 4

    (d) unsaturated

  5. Check: (c) and (d) match the names: ethane ("-ane") is saturated; ethene ("-ene") is unsaturated ✔.

  6. Answer (a) catenation (b) tetravalency (c) saturated (d) unsaturated

    Common trap: Swapping catenation and tetravalency. Catenation = bonding to itself; tetravalency = four bonds.

P8● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

Which ions in hard water react with soap to form scum?

hard water contains calcium and magnesium salts (Topic 8).

Soap itself is a sodium or potassium salt — these ions do not form scum.
CaX2+\ce{Ca^2+}CaX2+ and MgX2+\ce{Mg^2+}MgX2+ form insoluble salts with soap.
These negative ions are present but do not react with soap.
They are present in all water and are not the cause of hardness.

Asked: the ions responsible for scum.

Concept used: hard water contains calcium and magnesium salts (Topic 8).

  1. Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✘ Soap itself is a sodium or potassium salt — these ions do not form scum.
    • (b) ✔ CaX2+\ce{Ca^2+}CaX2+ and MgX2+\ce{Mg^2+}MgX2+ form insoluble salts with soap.
    • (c) ✘ These negative ions are present but do not react with soap.
    • (d) ✘ They are present in all water and are not the cause of hardness.

P9● FoundationTrue/False with justification · 1 markOriginal

True or false? Justify: "Ethanoic acid is a strong acid, because it turns blue litmus red."

Full solution

Given: a statement. Asked: true or false, with a reason.

Concept used: strong acids are completely ionised; carboxylic acids are weak (Topic 7).

  1. 1

    Turning blue litmus red shows that a substance is an acid — weak and strong acids both do this.

  2. 2

    Ethanoic acid is only partly ionised in water, so it is a weak acid (universal indicator shows a higher pH than hydrochloric acid).

  3. 3

    So the statement is false.

  4. Check: dilute hydrochloric acid also turns blue litmus red, yet the two acids give different universal-indicator colours ✔.

  5. Answer False. Litmus shows only that it is acidic; ethanoic acid is a weak acid because it is only partly ionised.

    Common trap: Using litmus to judge the strength of an acid. Litmus tells acid or base, not how strong.

P10●● StandardShort answer · 3 marksOriginal

(a) Why does carbon form covalent bonds instead of ionic bonds? (b) Methane is a gas at room temperature and does not conduct electricity. Explain both facts.

Full solution

Given: carbon; methane. Asked: why covalent; why a gas and a non-conductor.

Concept used: carbon cannot easily gain or lose four electrons; properties of covalent compounds (Topic 2).

  1. 1

    (a)

    Carbon (2, 4) needs four more electrons, or must lose four, to reach a noble-gas arrangement.

  2. 2

    Gaining four (CX4−\ce{C^4-}CX4−) is very difficult — 6 protons cannot hold 10 electrons easily.

  3. 3

    Losing four (CX4+\ce{C^4+}CX4+) needs a very large amount of energy.

  4. 4

    So carbon shares its four electrons — covalent bonds.

  5. 5

    (b)

    The forces between methane molecules are weak, so very little energy separates them → low boiling point (111 K) → a gas at room temperature.

  6. 6

    Methane has only shared electrons and no ions, so it cannot conduct electricity.

  7. Check: the same reasons apply to other covalent compounds in the textbook table — all have low melting and boiling points ✔.

  8. Answer (a) Gaining or losing four electrons is too difficult, so carbon shares them. (b) Weak forces between molecules → low boiling point (gas); no ions → no conduction.

    Common trap: Saying "the C–H bonds in methane are weak". The bonds inside the molecule are strong; it is the forces between molecules that are weak.

P11●● StandardShort answer · 3 marksOriginal

Draw the electron-dot structures of (a) methanol, CHX3OH\ce{CH3OH}CHX3​OH, and (b) ethyne, CX2HX2\ce{C2H2}CX2​HX2​. How many shared pairs are there in each molecule?

Full solution

Given: CHX3OH\ce{CH3OH}CHX3​OH; CX2HX2\ce{C2H2}CX2​HX2​. Asked: electron-dot structures; number of shared pairs.

Concept used: C shares 4 pairs, O 2, H 1; extra electrons stay as lone pairs (Topic 2).

  1. 1

    (a) Methanol

    Carbon shares one pair with each of three H and one pair with O.

  2. 2

    O shares one pair with C and one with H, and keeps two lone pairs.

    H∙×H∙×C×∙O∙∙∙∙∙∙H×∙H\begin{smallmatrix}&&\textstyle \mathrm{H}&&&&\\&&\textstyle \begin{smallmatrix}\bullet\\\times\end{smallmatrix}&&&&\\\textstyle \mathrm{H}&\textstyle \begin{smallmatrix}\bullet\times\end{smallmatrix}&\textstyle \mathrm{C}&\textstyle \begin{smallmatrix}\times\bullet\end{smallmatrix}&\textstyle \overset{\bullet\bullet}{\underset{\bullet\bullet}{\mathrm{O}}}&\textstyle \begin{smallmatrix}\bullet\bullet\end{smallmatrix}&\textstyle \mathrm{H}\\&&\textstyle \begin{smallmatrix}\times\\\bullet\end{smallmatrix}&&&&\\&&\textstyle \mathrm{H}&&&&\end{smallmatrix}H​∙×​​H∙×​C×∙​H​×∙​​∙∙O​∙∙​​∙∙​​H​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Shared pairs: 3 (C–H) + 1 (C–O) + 1 (O–H) = 5.

  4. 4

    (b) Ethyne

    Each C shares one pair with its H; each then still needs 3 → the carbons share three pairs.

    H∙×C××××××C×∙H\begin{smallmatrix}\textstyle \mathrm{H}&\textstyle \begin{smallmatrix}\bullet\times\end{smallmatrix}&\textstyle \mathrm{C}&\textstyle \begin{smallmatrix}\times\times\\\times\times\\\times\times\end{smallmatrix}&\textstyle \mathrm{C}&\textstyle \begin{smallmatrix}\times\bullet\end{smallmatrix}&\textstyle \mathrm{H}\end{smallmatrix}H​∙×​​C​××××××​​C​×∙​​H​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    Shared pairs: 1 + 3 + 1 = 5.

  6. Check: electrons drawn — methanol 4 + 6 + 4 × 1 = 14 = 5 shared pairs + 2 lone pairs ✔; ethyne 2 × 4 + 2 × 1 = 10 = 5 shared pairs ✔.

  7. Answer Structures as above; methanol 5 shared pairs (plus 2 lone pairs on O); ethyne 5 shared pairs (3 of them between the carbons).

    Common trap: Forgetting oxygen's lone pairs in methanol. Oxygen must show 8 electrons.

P12●● StandardShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

Name: (a) CHX3−CHX2−CHX2−CHX2−CHX2−Cl\ce{CH3-CH2-CH2-CH2-CH2-Cl}CHX3​−CHX2​−CHX2​−CHX2​−CHX2​−Cl (b) CHX3−CHX2−CHX2−OH\ce{CH3-CH2-CH2-OH}CHX3​−CHX2​−CHX2​−OH (c) CHX3−CHX2−COOH\ce{CH3-CH2-COOH}CHX3​−CHX2​−COOH (d) CHX2=CH−CHX2−CHX3\ce{CH2=CH-CH2-CH3}CHX2​=CH−CHX2​−CHX3​

Full solution

Given: four condensed formulae. Asked: names.

Concept used: the naming routine (Topic 5).

  1. 1

    (a) 5 carbons + –Cl (prefix) → chloropentane.

  2. 2

    (b) 3 carbons + –OH → propanol.

  3. 3

    (c) 2 + 1 (in –COOH) = 3 carbons + -oic acid → propanoic acid.

  4. 4

    (d) 4 carbons + C=C → butene.

  5. Check: formulae — (b) CX3HX8O\ce{C3H8O}CX3​HX8​O, (c) CX3HX6OX2\ce{C3H6O2}CX3​HX6​OX2​, (d) CX4HX8\ce{C4H8}CX4​HX8​, which fits CnH2n\mathrm{C}_n\mathrm{H}_{2n}Cn​H2n​ for an alkene ✔.

  6. Answer (a) chloropentane (b) propanol (c) propanoic acid (d) butene (full IUPAC names, beyond the syllabus: 1-chloropentane, propan-1-ol, but-1-ene)

    Common trap: Naming (c) "ethanoic acid" by not counting the carbon in –COOH.

P13●● StandardShort answer · 3 marksOriginal

A student named three compounds as shown. Say whether each name is right; correct it if it is wrong.
(a) CHX3−CO−CHX3\ce{CH3-CO-CH3}CHX3​−CO−CHX3​ — "propanal" (b) CHX3−CHX2−CHX2−CHO\ce{CH3-CH2-CH2-CHO}CHX3​−CHX2​−CHX2​−CHO — "propanal" (c) HCOOH\ce{HCOOH}HCOOH — "ethanoic acid"

Full solution

Given: three formulae with names. Asked: right or wrong; corrections.

Concept used: -al is an end –CHO; -one is an inside –CO–; count every carbon (Topic 5).

  1. 1

    (a) The C=O is on the middle carbon → ketone → propanone. "Propanal" is wrong.

  2. 2

    (b) Carbons: 3 + 1 (in –CHO) = 4 → butanal. "Propanal" is wrong — the –CHO carbon was not counted.

  3. 3

    (c) Only 1 carbon, in –COOH → methanoic acid. "Ethanoic acid" is wrong (that is CHX3COOH\ce{CH3COOH}CHX3​COOH).

  4. Check: rebuild each corrected name: propanone = 3 C with C=O in the middle ✔; butanal = 4 C with –CHO at the end ✔; methanoic acid = 1 C as –COOH ✔.

  5. Answer All three are wrong: (a) propanone (b) butanal (c) methanoic acid

    Common trap: Choosing between -al and -one by the formula's length. Look at where the C=O carbon is.

Name the type of each reaction and state the condition or reagent needed:

(a)CX2HX5OH+3 OX2→2 COX2+3 HX2O\text{(a)}\quad \ce{C2H5OH + 3O2 -> 2CO2 + 3H2O}(a)CX2​HX5​OH+3OX2​​2COX2​+3HX2​OSwipe to see the whole equation →
(b)CHX4+ClX2→CHX3Cl+HCl\text{(b)}\quad \ce{CH4 + Cl2 -> CH3Cl + HCl}(b)CHX4​+ClX2​​CHX3​Cl+HClSwipe to see the whole equation →
(c)CHX3−CH=CHX2+HX2→CHX3−CHX2−CHX3\text{(c)}\quad \ce{CH3-CH=CH2 + H2 -> CH3-CH2-CH3}(c)CHX3​−CH=CHX2​+HX2​​CHX3​−CHX2​−CHX3​Swipe to see the whole equation →
(d)CHX3CHX2OH+2 [O]→CHX3COOH+HX2O\text{(d)}\quad \ce{CH3CH2OH + 2[O] -> CH3COOH + H2O}(d)CHX3​CHX2​OH+2[O]​CHX3​COOH+HX2​OSwipe to see the whole equation →

Full solution

Given: four equations. Asked: reaction type and condition.

Concept used: the four reaction cards (Topic 6).

  1. 1

    (a) Burning in oxygen → combustion; needs a flame (ignition) and plenty of air.

  2. 2

    (b) Cl replaces H in a saturated hydrocarbon → substitution; needs sunlight.

  3. 3

    (c) HX2\ce{H2}HX2​ adds across C=C → addition (hydrogenation); needs a nickel or palladium catalyst.

  4. 4

    (d) Alcohol → carboxylic acid → oxidation; needs an oxidising agent — alkaline KMnOX4\ce{KMnO4}KMnOX4​ (or acidified KX2CrX2OX7\ce{K2Cr2O7}KX2​CrX2​OX7​) and heat.

  5. Check: (b) gives two products (one is HCl), as substitution should; (c) gives one product, as addition should ✔.

  6. Answer (a) combustion — oxygen, burning (b) substitution — sunlight (c) addition — Ni/Pd catalyst (d) oxidation — alkaline KMnOX4\ce{KMnO4}KMnOX4​ / acidified KX2CrX2OX7\ce{K2Cr2O7}KX2​CrX2​OX7​, heat

    Common trap: Calling (d) combustion. Combustion is complete burning to COX2\ce{CO2}COX2​ and water; (d) stops at the acid.

P15●● StandardShort answer · 3 marksOriginal

Complete and balance:
(a) CX2HX5OH+OX2→\ce{C2H5OH + O2 ->}CX2​HX5​OH+OX2​​
(b) CHX3COOH+NaX2COX3→\ce{CH3COOH + Na2CO3 ->}CHX3​COOH+NaX2​COX3​​
(c) CHX3COOCX2HX5+NaOH→\ce{CH3COOC2H5 + NaOH ->}CHX3​COOCX2​HX5​+NaOH​

Full solution

Given: three sets of reactants. Asked: complete, balanced equations.

Concept used: combustion; acid + carbonate; saponification (Topics 6–7).

  1. 1

    (a)

    Complete combustion → COX2\ce{CO2}COX2​ and HX2O\ce{H2O}HX2​O. Skeletal: CX2HX5OH+OX2→COX2+HX2O\ce{C2H5OH + O2 -> CO2 + H2O}CX2​HX5​OH+OX2​​COX2​+HX2​O

  2. 2

    Carbon: 2 → put 2 in front of COX2\ce{CO2}COX2​.

  3. 3

    Hydrogen: 6 → put 3 in front of HX2O\ce{H2O}HX2​O.

  4. 4

    Oxygen: right 4 + 3 = 7; left 1 from ethanol, so 6 more → 3 OX2\ce{O2}OX2​.

    CX2HX5OH+3 OX2→2 COX2+3 HX2O\ce{C2H5OH + 3O2 -> 2CO2 + 3H2O}CX2​HX5​OH+3OX2​​2COX2​+3HX2​OSwipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    (b)

    Acid + carbonate → salt + water + carbon dioxide. Sodium: right needs 2 → 2 CHX3COONa\ce{CH3COONa}CHX3​COONa, so 2 CHX3COOH\ce{CH3COOH}CHX3​COOH.

    2 CHX3COOH+NaX2COX3→2 CHX3COONa+HX2O+COX2\ce{2CH3COOH + Na2CO3 -> 2CH3COONa + H2O + CO2}2CHX3​COOH+NaX2​COX3​​2CHX3​COONa+HX2​O+COX2​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  6. 6

    (c)

    Ester + NaOH → alcohol + sodium salt (saponification); already balanced 1 : 1.

    CHX3COOCX2HX5+NaOH→CHX3COONa+CX2HX5OH\ce{CH3COOC2H5 + NaOH -> CH3COONa + C2H5OH}CHX3​COOCX2​HX5​+NaOH​CHX3​COONa+CX2​HX5​OHSwipe to see the whole equation →

  7. Check: (a) C 2 | 2, H 6 | 6, O 7 | 7 ✔ (b) C 5 | 5, H 8 | 8, O 7 | 7, Na 2 | 2 ✔ (c) C 4 | 4, H 9 | 9, O 3 | 3, Na 1 | 1 ✔.

  8. Answer The three balanced equations above.

    Common trap: In (a), forgetting the oxygen atom already in ethanol when counting oxygen.

P16●● StandardShort answer · 3 marksOriginal

The table shows three alcohols.

Alcohol Formula Molecular mass (u) Boiling point (about)
Methanol CHX3OH\ce{CH3OH}CHX3​OH 32 65 °C
Ethanol CX2HX5OH\ce{C2H5OH}CX2​HX5​OH 46 78 °C
Propanol CX3HX7OH\ce{C3H7OH}CX3​HX7​OH 60 97 °C

(a) By how much do the formulas and the molecular masses of successive members differ? (b) Predict the formula and molecular mass of the next member, and say whether its boiling point will be higher or lower than 97 °C. (c) Why do all of them react with sodium in the same way?

Full solution

Given: formulas, masses, boiling points. Asked: (a)–(c).

Concept used: homologous series (Topic 4).

  1. 1

    (a) Each formula differs by CHX2\ce{CH2}CHX2​; each mass by 46 − 32 = 60 − 46 = 14 u.

  2. 2

    (b) Next member: CX3HX7OH\ce{C3H7OH}CX3​HX7​OH + CHX2\ce{CH2}CHX2​ = CX4HX9OH\ce{C4H9OH}CX4​HX9​OH; mass 60 + 14 = 74 u.

  3. 3

    Boiling points rise along the series as molecular mass increases → higher than 97 °C.

  4. 4

    (c) All have the same functional group, –OH, which decides the chemical properties.

  5. Check: 4 × 12 + 10 × 1 + 16 = 74 u ✔ — the same answer by adding up atomic masses.

  6. Answer (a) CHX2\ce{CH2}CHX2​ and 14 u (b) CX4HX9OH\ce{C4H9OH}CX4​HX9​OH (butanol), 74 u, boiling point higher (c) same –OH group → similar chemical properties

    Common trap: Predicting the boiling point by adding exactly the same number of degrees each step. The trend is upward, but not by a fixed amount.

P17●● StandardShort answer · 3 marksOriginal

Water from a hand-pump contains calcium chloride. (a) Why does soap give very little lather with it? Write an equation, using sodium stearate, CX17HX35COONa\ce{C17H35COONa}CX17​HX35​COONa, as the soap. (b) Why does a detergent lather well in the same water?

Full solution

Given: hard water with CaClX2\ce{CaCl2}CaClX2​; soap; detergent. Asked: (a) reason and equation; (b) reason.

Concept used: scum formation; detergents in hard water (Topic 8).

  1. 1

    (a)

    CaX2+\ce{Ca^2+}CaX2+ ions react with the soap to form calcium stearate, which is insoluble — scum.

  2. 2

    Soap is used up in forming scum, so little is left to make lather.

  3. 3

    One CaX2+\ce{Ca^2+}CaX2+ needs two stearate ions → 2 CX17HX35COONa\ce{C17H35COONa}CX17​HX35​COONa:

    2 CX17HX35COONa+CaClX2→(CX17HX35COO)X2Ca↓+2 NaCl\ce{2C17H35COONa + CaCl2 -> (C17H35COO)2Ca v + 2NaCl}2CX17​HX35​COONa+CaClX2​​(CX17​HX35​COO)X2​Ca↓+2NaClSwipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    (b)

    The charged ends of detergent molecules do not form insoluble precipitates with CaX2+\ce{Ca^2+}CaX2+, so the detergent stays free to lather and clean.

  5. Check: C 36 | 36, H 70 | 70, O 4 | 4, Na 2 | 2, Ca 1 | 1, Cl 2 | 2 ✔.

  6. Answer (a) Calcium ions form insoluble scum with soap, wasting it (equation in step 3) (b) detergents form no insoluble precipitate with calcium ions.

    Common trap: Writing CX17HX35COOCa\ce{C17H35COOCa}CX17​HX35​COOCa. Calcium is CaX2+\ce{Ca^2+}CaX2+, so it needs two stearate ions.

P18●● StandardShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

Which of these pairs are structural isomers? Give a reason for each.
(a) CHX3−CHX2−CHX2−OH\ce{CH3-CH2-CH2-OH}CHX3​−CHX2​−CHX2​−OH and CHX3−CH(OH)−CHX3\ce{CH3-CH(OH)-CH3}CHX3​−CH(OH)−CHX3​
(b) CHX3−CHX2−CHO\ce{CH3-CH2-CHO}CHX3​−CHX2​−CHO and CHX3−CO−CHX3\ce{CH3-CO-CH3}CHX3​−CO−CHX3​
(c) CHX3−CHX2−OH\ce{CH3-CH2-OH}CHX3​−CHX2​−OH and CHX3−CHX2−CHX2−OH\ce{CH3-CH2-CH2-OH}CHX3​−CHX2​−CHX2​−OH
(d) CHX3−CHX3\ce{CH3-CH3}CHX3​−CHX3​ and CHX2=CHX2\ce{CH2=CH2}CHX2​=CHX2​

Full solution

Given: four pairs. Asked: which are isomers.

Concept used: isomers = same molecular formula, different structures (Topic 3).

  1. 1

    (a) Both CX3HX8O\ce{C3H8O}CX3​HX8​O; –OH on an end carbon vs the middle carbon → isomers.

  2. 2

    (b) Both CX3HX6O\ce{C3H6O}CX3​HX6​O; aldehyde vs ketone → isomers.

  3. 3

    (c) CX2HX6O\ce{C2H6O}CX2​HX6​O and CX3HX8O\ce{C3H8O}CX3​HX8​O — different formulas; they differ by CHX2\ce{CH2}CHX2​ → not isomers (they are homologues).

  4. 4

    (d) CX2HX6\ce{C2H6}CX2​HX6​ and CX2HX4\ce{C2H4}CX2​HX4​ — different formulas → not isomers.

  5. Check: count atoms in each formula, as done above; only (a) and (b) match ✔.

  6. Answer (a) and (b) are isomers; (c) are homologues; (d) are neither.

    Common trap: Calling (c) isomers because both are alcohols. Isomers must have the same molecular formula.

P19●● StandardShort answer · 3 marksOriginal

A student drew these electron-dot structures for oxygen and nitrogen. Find the error in each and draw the correct structures.

Student's OX2\ce{O2}OX2​:

O∙∙∙∙∙×O××××\begin{smallmatrix}\textstyle \overset{\bullet\bullet}{\underset{\bullet\bullet}{\mathrm{O}}}&\textstyle \begin{smallmatrix}\bullet\times\end{smallmatrix}&\textstyle \overset{\times\times}{\underset{\times\times}{\mathrm{O}}}\end{smallmatrix}∙∙O​∙∙​​∙×​​××O​××​​Swipe to see the whole equation →

Student's NX2\ce{N2}NX2​:

∙∙N∙×∙×N××\begin{smallmatrix}\textstyle {}^{\bullet}_{\bullet}\mathrm{N}&\textstyle \begin{smallmatrix}\bullet\times\\\bullet\times\end{smallmatrix}&\textstyle \mathrm{N}{}^{\times}_{\times}\end{smallmatrix}∙∙​N​∙×∙×​​N××​​Swipe to see the whole equation →

Full solution

Given: two drawings. Asked: errors; correct structures.

Concept used: count electrons round each atom — each must have 8 (Topic 2).

  1. 1

    Oxygen

    Each O in the drawing has 4 lone + 2 shared = 6 electrons, and only 5 of its own 6 valence electrons are shown → wrong.

  2. 2

    Each O needs 2 → share two pairs (double bond), keeping two lone pairs:

    O∙∙∙∙∙×∙×O××××\begin{smallmatrix}\textstyle \overset{\bullet\bullet}{\underset{\bullet\bullet}{\mathrm{O}}}&\textstyle \begin{smallmatrix}\bullet\times\\\bullet\times\end{smallmatrix}&\textstyle \overset{\times\times}{\underset{\times\times}{\mathrm{O}}}\end{smallmatrix}∙∙O​∙∙​​∙×∙×​​××O​××​​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    Nitrogen

    Each N in the drawing has 2 lone + 4 shared = 6 electrons → wrong.

  4. 4

    Each N needs 3 → share three pairs (triple bond), keeping one lone pair:

    ∙∙N∙×∙×∙×N××\begin{smallmatrix}\textstyle {}^{\bullet}_{\bullet}\mathrm{N}&\textstyle \begin{smallmatrix}\bullet\times\\\bullet\times\\\bullet\times\end{smallmatrix}&\textstyle \mathrm{N}{}^{\times}_{\times}\end{smallmatrix}∙∙​N​∙×∙×∙×​​N××​​Swipe to see the whole equation →

  5. Check: corrected OX2\ce{O2}OX2​ — 12 electrons drawn = 2 × 6 ✔, 8 round each O ✔; corrected NX2\ce{N2}NX2​ — 10 electrons = 2 × 5 ✔, 8 round each N ✔.

  6. Answer OX2\ce{O2}OX2​ needs a double bond (2 shared pairs); NX2\ce{N2}NX2​ needs a triple bond (3 shared pairs). Correct structures above.

    Common trap: "Fixing" the drawing by adding extra lone pairs. The number of electrons is fixed; only sharing more of them gives each atom 8.

P20●● StandardShort answer · 3 marksOriginal

Compounds P and Q both have the formula CX4HX8O\ce{C4H8O}CX4​HX8​O. P is an aldehyde and Q is a ketone with a straight chain. Draw their structures, name them and name their functional groups.

Full solution

Given: CX4HX8O\ce{C4H8O}CX4​HX8​O; P aldehyde; Q ketone. Asked: structures, names, functional groups.

Concept used: –CHO at a chain end; –CO– inside a chain (Topics 4–5).

    P: four carbons with –CHO at the end:

    HHHH∣∣∣∣H−C−C−C−C=−O∣∣∣HHH\def\arraystretch{0.6}\begin{array}{ccccccccccc}&&\mathclap{\mathrm{H}}&&\mathclap{\mathrm{H}}&&\mathclap{\mathrm{H}}&&\mathclap{\mathrm{H}}&&\\&&\mathclap{\vert}&&\mathclap{\vert}&&\mathclap{\vert}&&\mathclap{\vert}&&\\\mathclap{\mathrm{H}}&\mathclap{-}&\mathclap{\mathrm{C}}&\mathclap{-}&\mathclap{\mathrm{C}}&\mathclap{-}&\mathclap{\mathrm{C}}&\mathclap{-}&\mathclap{\mathrm{C}}&\mathclap{\mathclap{=}\vphantom{-}}&\mathclap{\mathrm{O}}\\&&\mathclap{\vert}&&\mathclap{\vert}&&\mathclap{\vert}&&&&\\&&\mathclap{\mathrm{H}}&&\mathclap{\mathrm{H}}&&\mathclap{\mathrm{H}}&&&&\end{array}H​−​H∣C∣H​−​H∣C∣H​−​H∣C∣H​−​H∣C​=−​O​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Name: butanal; group: aldehyde (–CHO).

  3. 3

    Q: four carbons with C=O on the second carbon:

    HOHH∣∥∣∣H−C−C−C−C−H∣∣∣HHH\def\arraystretch{0.6}\begin{array}{ccccccccccc}&&\mathclap{\mathrm{H}}&&\mathclap{\mathrm{O}}&&\mathclap{\mathrm{H}}&&\mathclap{\mathrm{H}}&&\\&&\mathclap{\vert}&&\mathclap{\Vert}&&\mathclap{\vert}&&\mathclap{\vert}&&\\\mathclap{\mathrm{H}}&\mathclap{-}&\mathclap{\mathrm{C}}&\mathclap{-}&\mathclap{\mathrm{C}}&\mathclap{-}&\mathclap{\mathrm{C}}&\mathclap{-}&\mathclap{\mathrm{C}}&\mathclap{-}&\mathclap{\mathrm{H}}\\&&\mathclap{\vert}&&&&\mathclap{\vert}&&\mathclap{\vert}&&\\&&\mathclap{\mathrm{H}}&&&&\mathclap{\mathrm{H}}&&\mathclap{\mathrm{H}}&&\end{array}H​−​H∣C∣H​−​O∥C​−​H∣C∣H​−​H∣C∣H​−​H​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    Name: butanone; group: ketone (–CO–).

  5. Check: both drawings have C 4, H 8, O 1 ✔. Moving Q's C=O to the third carbon gives the same molecule read from the other end, so a straight-chain ketone with four carbons has only one structure ✔.

P21●● StandardShort answer · 3 marksOriginal

Methanol, CHX3OH\ce{CH3OH}CHX3​OH, is warmed with ethanoic acid and a few drops of concentrated sulphuric acid. (a) Write the equation and name the type of reaction. (b) What is the role of the sulphuric acid? (c) What happens when the product is boiled with sodium hydroxide solution? Write the equation.

Full solution

Given: methanol + ethanoic acid (acid catalyst); then the product + NaOH. Asked: (a)–(c).

Concept used: esterification and saponification (Topic 7). Why it applies: an alcohol and a carboxylic acid react just as ethanol and ethanoic acid do.

  1. 1

    (a)

    The acid's –OH and the alcohol's H leave as water; the ester methyl ethanoate forms:

    CHX3COOH+CHX3OH→acidCHX3COOCHX3+HX2O\ce{CH3COOH + CH3OH ->[\text{acid}] CH3COOCH3 + H2O}CHX3​COOH+CHX3​OHacid​CHX3​COOCHX3​+HX2​OSwipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Type: esterification.

  3. 3

    (b)

    Concentrated HX2SOX4\ce{H2SO4}HX2​SOX4​ acts as an acid catalyst.

  4. 4

    (c)

    The ester is split into the alcohol and the sodium salt of the acid — saponification:

    CHX3COOCHX3+NaOH→CHX3COONa+CHX3OH\ce{CH3COOCH3 + NaOH -> CH3COONa + CH3OH}CHX3​COOCHX3​+NaOH​CHX3​COONa+CHX3​OHSwipe to see the whole equation →

  5. Check: (a) C 3 | 3, H 8 | 6 + 2, O 3 | 2 + 1 ✔ (c) C 3 | 3, H 7 | 3 + 4, O 3 | 2 + 1, Na 1 | 1 ✔. Reaction (c) returns the methanol used in (a) ✔.

  6. Answer (a) esterification (equation in step 1) (b) acid catalyst (c) saponification (equation in step 4)

    Common trap: Calling the sulphuric acid a dehydrating agent here. That is its job when ethanol alone is heated at 443 K.

A spatula of sodium carbonate is added to 2 mL of dilute ethanoic acid in a test tube, and the gas is passed through lime water. (a) What do you observe in each tube? (b) Write the equations for both reactions. (c) What would you observe if ethanol were used instead of ethanoic acid?

Full solution

Given: ethanoic acid + NaX2COX3\ce{Na2CO3}NaX2​COX3​; gas → lime water. Asked: (a)–(c).

Concept used: acid + carbonate → salt + water + COX2\ce{CO2}COX2​; lime water test (Topic 7).

  1. 1

    (a) Reaction tube: brisk effervescence. Lime water: turns milky.

  2. 2

    (b)

    2 CHX3COOH+NaX2COX3→2 CHX3COONa+HX2O+COX2\ce{2CH3COOH + Na2CO3 -> 2CH3COONa + H2O + CO2}2CHX3​COOH+NaX2​COX3​​2CHX3​COONa+HX2​O+COX2​Swipe to see the whole equation →
    Ca(OH)X2+COX2→CaCOX3+HX2O\ce{Ca(OH)2 + CO2 -> CaCO3 + H2O}Ca(OH)X2​+COX2​​CaCOX3​+HX2​OSwipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    The milkiness is insoluble calcium carbonate.

  4. 4

    (c) Ethanol is not an acid → no effervescence, and the lime water stays clear.

  5. Check: first equation — C 6 | 6, H 8 | 8, O 7 | 7, Na 2 | 2 ✔; second — Ca 1 | 1, O 4 | 4, H 2 | 2, C 1 | 1 ✔.

  6. Answer (a) fizzing; lime water turns milky (b) equations above (c) no reaction with ethanol.

P23●● StandardShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

(a) Naphthalene burns with a yellow, sooty flame but an LPG stove burns with a blue flame. Give a reason. (b) What does a blackened vessel bottom tell you about the stove?

Full solution

Given: two flames; a blackened vessel. Asked: reasons.

Concept used: saturated vs unsaturated compounds; incomplete combustion (Topic 6).

  1. 1

    (a) Naphthalene is an unsaturated compound; such compounds give a yellow flame with lots of black smoke.

  2. 2

    LPG (mainly butane and propane) is saturated, and the stove mixes it with plenty of air → complete combustion → clean blue flame.

  3. 3

    (b) Soot on the vessel shows incomplete combustion: the air holes are blocked, so not enough air mixes with the fuel, and fuel is wasted.

  4. Check: both answers match the rule: soot = carbon that did not burn = not enough oxygen for the fuel ✔.

  5. Answer (a) naphthalene is unsaturated (sooty flame); LPG is saturated and burns with enough air (blue flame) (b) incomplete combustion — air holes blocked, fuel wasted.

    Common trap: "Yellow flames are hotter." Yellow light comes from glowing soot — a sign of incomplete burning.

P24●● StandardShort answer · 3 marksOriginal

(a) Describe the arrangement of soap molecules in a micelle formed in water around an oil droplet. (b) Why are the molecules arranged in this way? (c) How would the arrangement differ if the soap were dissolved in kerosene, an oily liquid?

Full solution

Given: soap in water and in kerosene. Asked: (a)–(c).

Concept used: hydrophobic tail, hydrophilic head (Topic 8).

  1. 1

    (a) Soap molecules surround the oil droplet in a ball: tails pointing inwards into the oil, ionic heads on the outside facing the water.

  2. 2

    (b) The hydrocarbon tail is hydrophobic — it mixes with oil, not water; the ionic head is hydrophilic — it interacts with water.

  3. 3

    (c) In kerosene the solvent is oily, so the arrangement is reversed: the ionic heads cluster in the middle and the tails face outwards into the kerosene.

  4. Check: in each case, each end of the molecule faces the substance it mixes with ✔.

  5. Answer (a) tails in the oil, heads outside in water (b) tails are hydrophobic, heads hydrophilic (c) reversed — heads inside, tails outside.

    Common trap: Drawing the water micelle with heads inside — that is the kerosene arrangement.

P25●●● AdvancedCase/source-based · 4 marksOriginal

Case: Three steps from one alcohol

An alcohol A, CX3HX8O\ce{C3H8O}CX3​HX8​O, with its –OH on an end carbon, is warmed with alkaline potassium permanganate and gives B, CX3HX6OX2\ce{C3H6O2}CX3​HX6​OX2​. When A and B are warmed together with a few drops of concentrated sulphuric acid, a fruity-smelling compound C forms. Boiling C with sodium hydroxide solution gives back A, together with a salt D.

(a) Name A and B. (1)
(b) To which class of compounds does C belong? Write the equation for its formation. (1)
(c) Name the reaction C → A + D and write its equation. (1)
(d) What role does the alkaline potassium permanganate play? (1)

Full solution

Given: A (CX3HX8O\ce{C3H8O}CX3​HX8​O) → B (CX3HX6OX2\ce{C3H6O2}CX3​HX6​OX2​) → C (with A) → A + D. Asked: (a)–(d).

Concept used: oxidation of alcohols; esterification; saponification (Topics 6–7).

  1. 1

    (a)

    A is a three-carbon alcohol → propanol, CHX3CHX2CHX2OH\ce{CH3CH2CH2OH}CHX3​CHX2​CHX2​OH.

  2. 2

    Oxidation gives the acid with the same number of carbons → B = propanoic acid, CHX3CHX2COOH\ce{CH3CH2COOH}CHX3​CHX2​COOH (CX3HX6OX2\ce{C3H6O2}CX3​HX6​OX2​ ✔).

  3. 3

    (b)

    Acid + alcohol with an acid catalyst → a fruity-smelling ester:

    CHX3CHX2COOH+CHX3CHX2CHX2OH→acidCHX3CHX2COOCHX2CHX2CHX3+HX2O\ce{CH3CH2COOH + CH3CH2CH2OH ->[\text{acid}] CH3CH2COOCH2CH2CH3 + H2O}CHX3​CHX2​COOH+CHX3​CHX2​CHX2​OHacid​CHX3​CHX2​COOCHX2​CHX2​CHX3​+HX2​OSwipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    (c)

    Ester + NaOH → alcohol + sodium salt → saponification; D = sodium propanoate:

    CHX3CHX2COOCHX2CHX2CHX3+NaOH→CHX3CHX2COONa+CHX3CHX2CHX2OH\ce{CH3CH2COOCH2CH2CH3 + NaOH -> CH3CH2COONa + CH3CH2CH2OH}CHX3​CHX2​COOCHX2​CHX2​CHX3​+NaOH​CHX3​CHX2​COONa+CHX3​CHX2​CHX2​OHSwipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    (d)

    It adds oxygen to propanol → oxidising agent.

  6. Check: (b) C 6 | 6, H 14 | 12 + 2, O 3 | 2 + 1 ✔; (c) C 6 | 6, H 13 | 5 + 8, O 3 | 2 + 1, Na 1 | 1 ✔. A returns at the end, as the case says ✔.

  7. Answer (a) A propanol, B propanoic acid (b) an ester; equation above (c) saponification; equation above (d) oxidising agent

    Common trap: Making B with a different number of carbons. Oxidation changes −CHX2OH\ce{-CH2OH}−CHX2​OH to −COOH\ce{-COOH}−COOH; the chain length stays the same.

P26●●● AdvancedCase/source-based · 4 marksOriginal

Case: Oil or ghee?

Ritika compares two cooking fats at home. A bottle of groundnut oil says "rich in unsaturated fatty acids". A tin of vanaspati says "made from vegetable oils by hydrogenation". The oil is liquid; the vanaspati is solid.

(a) Name the reaction used to make vanaspati and the catalyst needed. (1)
(b) What happens to the carbon–carbon double bonds in the oil during this reaction? (1)
(c) Your textbook gives a test to tell a saturated hydrocarbon from an unsaturated one. Describe it, with the result for each. (1)
(d) According to your textbook, which of the two is the better choice for everyday cooking, and why? (1)

Full solution

Given: an unsaturated oil; a hydrogenated fat. Asked: (a)–(d).

Concept used: addition of hydrogen; tests for unsaturation; health note (Topic 6).

  1. 1

    (a) Hydrogenation (an addition reaction), with a nickel catalyst.

  2. 2

    (b) Hydrogen atoms add across the C=C double bonds, turning them into single bonds — the chains become saturated.

  3. 3

    (c) Burn each with plenty of air: the saturated hydrocarbon gives a clean blue flame, the unsaturated one a yellow, sooty flame.

  4. 4

    (d) The oil: fats with saturated fatty acids are said to be harmful to health, so oils with unsaturated fatty acids should be chosen for cooking.

  5. Check: (b) explains the label in (a): "hydrogenation" = adding hydrogen to the double bonds ✔.

  6. Answer (a) hydrogenation, nickel (b) double bonds become single bonds (saturated) (c) clean blue flame (saturated) vs yellow sooty flame (unsaturated) (d) the oil — unsaturated fatty acids are the healthier choice.

    Common trap: Writing "substitution" in (a). Hydrogen is added — nothing is replaced.

(a) Draw two straight-chain alcohols with the formula CX4HX10O\ce{C4H10O}CX4​HX10​O. (2)
(b) Your textbook would call both of them "butanol". Are they the same compound? Explain. (1)
(c) Would you expect both to react with sodium? Give a reason. (1)
(d) A student says, "Every isomer of CX4HX10O\ce{C4H10O}CX4​HX10​O must be an alcohol." Is the student right? (1)

Full solution

Given: CX4HX10O\ce{C4H10O}CX4​HX10​O. Asked: (a)–(d).

Concept used: position isomers; functional groups decide chemical properties (Topics 3–5).

  1. 1

    (a)

    Four carbons in a chain with –OH on an end carbon:

    HHHH∣∣∣∣H−C−C−C−C−O−H∣∣∣∣HHHH\def\arraystretch{0.6}\begin{array}{ccccccccccccc}&&\mathclap{\mathrm{H}}&&\mathclap{\mathrm{H}}&&\mathclap{\mathrm{H}}&&\mathclap{\mathrm{H}}&&&&\\&&\mathclap{\vert}&&\mathclap{\vert}&&\mathclap{\vert}&&\mathclap{\vert}&&&&\\\mathclap{\mathrm{H}}&\mathclap{-}&\mathclap{\mathrm{C}}&\mathclap{-}&\mathclap{\mathrm{C}}&\mathclap{-}&\mathclap{\mathrm{C}}&\mathclap{-}&\mathclap{\mathrm{C}}&\mathclap{-}&\mathclap{\mathrm{O}}&\mathclap{-}&\mathclap{\mathrm{H}}\\&&\mathclap{\vert}&&\mathclap{\vert}&&\mathclap{\vert}&&\mathclap{\vert}&&&&\\&&\mathclap{\mathrm{H}}&&\mathclap{\mathrm{H}}&&\mathclap{\mathrm{H}}&&\mathclap{\mathrm{H}}&&&&\end{array}H​−​H∣C∣H​−​H∣C∣H​−​H∣C∣H​−​H∣C∣H​−​O​−​H​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  2. 2

    Four carbons with –OH on the second carbon:

    HHHH∣∣∣∣H−C−C−C−C−H∣∣∣∣HOHH∣H\def\arraystretch{0.6}\begin{array}{ccccccccccc}&&\mathclap{\mathrm{H}}&&\mathclap{\mathrm{H}}&&\mathclap{\mathrm{H}}&&\mathclap{\mathrm{H}}&&\\&&\mathclap{\vert}&&\mathclap{\vert}&&\mathclap{\vert}&&\mathclap{\vert}&&\\\mathclap{\mathrm{H}}&\mathclap{-}&\mathclap{\mathrm{C}}&\mathclap{-}&\mathclap{\mathrm{C}}&\mathclap{-}&\mathclap{\mathrm{C}}&\mathclap{-}&\mathclap{\mathrm{C}}&\mathclap{-}&\mathclap{\mathrm{H}}\\&&\mathclap{\vert}&&\mathclap{\vert}&&\mathclap{\vert}&&\mathclap{\vert}&&\\&&\mathclap{\mathrm{H}}&&\mathclap{\mathrm{O}}&&\mathclap{\mathrm{H}}&&\mathclap{\mathrm{H}}&&\\&&&&\mathclap{\vert}&&&&&&\\&&&&\mathclap{\mathrm{H}}&&&&&&\end{array}H​−​H∣C∣H​−​H∣C∣O∣H​−​H∣C∣H​−​H∣C∣H​−​H​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    (b)

    No — the –OH is on different carbons, so the structures differ: they are structural isomers. (Beyond the syllabus, their full names are butan-1-ol and butan-2-ol.)

  4. 4

    (c)

    Yes — both contain the –OH group, and alcohols react with sodium to give hydrogen.

  5. 5

    (d)

    No. The same atoms can also be arranged with the oxygen between two carbons (for example CHX3−O−CHX2−CHX2−CHX3\ce{CH3-O-CH2-CH2-CH3}CHX3​−O−CHX2​−CHX2​−CHX3​), which is not an alcohol. (Such compounds, called ethers, are beyond the syllabus.) An isomer only needs the same molecular formula.

  6. Check: each drawing in (a) has C 4, H 10, O 1 and four bonds at every carbon ✔.

  7. Answer (a) the two structures above (b) different compounds — position isomers (c) yes, both have –OH (d) no — isomers can belong to different families.

P28●●● AdvancedShort answer · 4 marksOriginal

Evaluate each statement. Say whether it is correct, and correct it if it is not.

  • Arnav: "Hydrogenation of an alkene needs sunlight."
  • Bela: "When ethanol is heated at 443 K with excess concentrated sulphuric acid, the acid is a catalyst."
  • Chirag: "Alkaline potassium permanganate is used up when it oxidises ethanol."
  • Divya: "Methane reacts with chlorine in sunlight by addition, because chlorine atoms join the molecule."

Full solution

Given: four statements about reactions. Asked: verdict and correction.

Concept used: conditions and roles in the reaction types (Topics 6–7).

  1. 1

    Arnav — incorrect. Hydrogenation needs a nickel or palladium catalyst. Sunlight is the condition for substitution with chlorine.

  2. 2

    Bela — incorrect. Here the acid removes water from ethanol: it is a dehydrating agent. (It acts as a catalyst in esterification.)

  3. 3

    Chirag — correct. An oxidising agent is used up; that is why the purple colour disappears until all the ethanol has reacted.

  4. 4

    Divya — incorrect. Methane is saturated; chlorine replaces a hydrogen atom and HCl forms → substitution:

    CHX4+ClX2→sunlightCHX3Cl+HCl\ce{CH4 + Cl2 ->[\text{sunlight}] CH3Cl + HCl}CHX4​+ClX2​sunlight​CHX3​Cl+HClSwipe to see the whole equation →

  5. Check: the equation has two products — the sign of substitution — and balances: C 1 | 1, H 4 | 3 + 1, Cl 2 | 1 + 1 ✔.

  6. Answer Arnav wrong (Ni/Pd); Bela wrong (dehydrating agent); Chirag right; Divya wrong (substitution).

    Common trap: Deciding "addition" whenever a new atom appears in the product. In substitution a new atom appears too — but another atom leaves.

P29●●● AdvancedCase/source-based · 4 marksOriginal

Case: The hostel laundry

A school hostel gets its water from a deep tube-well. The washerman finds that bars of soap get used up quickly, clothes come out with grey patches, and a white, curdy scum sticks to the sides of the buckets. A visitor suggests switching to a detergent powder.

(a) What does the evidence tell you about the water? (1)
(b) What are the grey patches and the white crust? Which ions cause them? (1)
(c) Explain why the detergent will help. (1)
(d) The washerman also beats the clothes on a stone. How does this help the cleaning? (1)

Full solution

Given: tube-well water; soap wasted; grey patches; crust. Asked: (a)–(d).

Concept used: hard water, scum, detergents, agitation (Topic 8).

  1. 1

    (a) The water is hard — it contains calcium and magnesium salts.

  2. 2

    (b) They are scum — insoluble compounds formed when CaX2+\ce{Ca^2+}CaX2+ and MgX2+\ce{Mg^2+}MgX2+ ions react with soap.

  3. 3

    (c) The charged ends of detergent molecules do not form insoluble precipitates with calcium and magnesium ions, so no scum forms and the detergent keeps cleaning.

  4. 4

    (d) Beating loosens the oily dirt and breaks it into small droplets that soap or detergent molecules can surround as micelles, which are then rinsed away.

  5. Check: every clue in the case — soap used up fast, grey deposits, crust — is explained by one cause, hard water forming scum ✔.

  6. Answer (a) hard water (b) scum, from CaX2+\ce{Ca^2+}CaX2+/MgX2+\ce{Mg^2+}MgX2+ (c) detergents form no scum (d) agitation helps form micelles and dislodges dirt.

    Common trap: Saying the detergent "softens" the water. It does not remove the calcium and magnesium ions; it simply does not react with them.

P30●●● AdvancedCase/source-based · 4 marksOriginal

Case: Boiling points of alkanes

Alkane Formula Boiling point
Methane CHX4\ce{CH4}CHX4​ −162 °C
Ethane CX2HX6\ce{C2H6}CX2​HX6​ −89 °C
Propane CX3HX8\ce{C3H8}CX3​HX8​ −42 °C
Butane CX4HX10\ce{C4H10}CX4​HX10​ −1 °C
Pentane CX5HX12\ce{C5H12}CX5​HX12​ 36 °C

(a) Describe the trend in boiling point and explain it. (1)
(b) Which of these alkanes are gases at a room temperature of 25 °C? (1)
(c) LPG cylinders contain mainly propane and butane, kept liquid under pressure. Using the data, explain why LPG turns into a gas as soon as it leaves the cylinder. (1)
(d) Will hexane, CX6HX14\ce{C6H14}CX6​HX14​, have a higher or lower boiling point than pentane? Will it be a gas or a liquid at room temperature? (1)

Full solution

Given: boiling points of five alkanes. Asked: (a)–(d).

Concept used: gradation of physical properties in a homologous series (Topic 4).

  1. 1

    (a) Boiling point rises with each extra CHX2\ce{CH2}CHX2​, because molecular mass increases along the series.

  2. 2

    (b) A substance is a gas if its boiling point is below 25 °C → methane, ethane, propane and butane.

  3. 3

    (c) Propane (−42 °C) and butane (−1 °C) boil well below room temperature; once the pressure is released, they boil and become gas.

  4. 4

    (d) Hexane is the next member → higher boiling point than 36 °C → a liquid at 25 °C.

  5. Check: pentane (36 °C) is the first member above 25 °C, so every member after it, including hexane, is also a liquid at room temperature ✔.

  6. Answer (a) rises with molecular mass (b) methane, ethane, propane, butane (c) their boiling points are below room temperature (d) higher; liquid.

    Common trap: Reading "−42 °C" as higher than "−1 °C". On a thermometer, −42 °C is much colder.

E10●● StandardShort answer · 3 marksNCERT Exemplar Ch4 SA 42

Catenation is the ability of an atom to form bonds with other atoms of the same element. It is exhibited by both carbon and silicon. Compare the ability of catenation of the two elements. Give reasons.

Full solution

Given: carbon and silicon both show catenation. Asked: compare; reasons.

Concept used: bond strength depends on atom size (Topic 3).

  1. 1

    Carbon shows catenation to a far greater extent: very long chains, branches and rings.

  2. 2

    Silicon forms chains of only about seven or eight atoms, and these compounds are very reactive.

  3. 3

    Reason: the carbon atom is small, so its nucleus holds the shared electron pairs strongly — the C–C bond is strong and stable.

  4. 4

    The silicon atom is larger, so the Si–Si bond is much weaker.

  5. Check: this agrees with the official answer: carbon's smaller size makes C–C bonds strong; Si–Si bonds are weaker because of its larger size ✔.

  6. Answer Carbon catenates far more than silicon because its small size gives strong, stable C–C bonds; silicon's larger atoms form weaker Si–Si bonds, so its chains are short and reactive.

    Common trap: Saying silicon "cannot" catenate. It can — only to a much smaller extent.

E11●● StandardLong answer · 5 marksNCERT Exemplar Ch4 LA 52

A compound C (molecular formula, CX2HX4OX2\ce{C2H4O2}CX2​HX4​OX2​) reacts with Na - metal to form a compound R and evolves a gas which burns with a pop sound. Compound C on treatment with an alcohol A in presence of an acid forms a sweet smelling compound S (molecular formula, CX3HX6OX2\ce{C3H6O2}CX3​HX6​OX2​). On addition of NaOH to C, it also gives R and water. S on treatment with NaOH solution gives back R and A.
Identify C, R, A, S and write down the reactions involved.

Full solution

Given: C = CX2HX4OX2\ce{C2H4O2}CX2​HX4​OX2​; C + Na → R + gas (pop); C + A → S (CX3HX6OX2\ce{C3H6O2}CX3​HX6​OX2​, sweet); C + NaOH → R + water; S + NaOH → R + A. Asked: C, R, A, S; equations.

Concept used: reactions of ethanoic acid; esterification; saponification (Topic 7).

  1. 1

    CX2HX4OX2\ce{C2H4O2}CX2​HX4​OX2​, an acid → C = ethanoic acid, CHX3COOH\ce{CH3COOH}CHX3​COOH.

  2. 2

    With sodium, the gas that pops is hydrogen, and R is its sodium salt → R = sodium ethanoate:

    2 CHX3COOH+2 Na→2 CHX3COONa+HX2\ce{2CH3COOH + 2Na -> 2CH3COONa + H2}2CHX3​COOH+2Na​2CHX3​COONa+HX2​Swipe to see the whole equation →
  3. 3

    S is an ester with 3 carbons; ethanoic acid supplies 2 → the alcohol has 1 carbon → A = methanol, and S = methyl ethanoate:

    CHX3COOH+CHX3OH→acidCHX3COOCHX3+HX2O\ce{CH3COOH + CH3OH ->[\text{acid}] CH3COOCH3 + H2O}CHX3​COOH+CHX3​OHacid​CHX3​COOCHX3​+HX2​OSwipe to see the whole equation →
  4. 4

    C + NaOH gives R and water (neutralisation):

    CHX3COOH+NaOH→CHX3COONa+HX2O\ce{CH3COOH + NaOH -> CH3COONa + H2O}CHX3​COOH+NaOH​CHX3​COONa+HX2​OSwipe to see the whole equation →
  5. 5

    S + NaOH gives back R and A (saponification):

    CHX3COOCHX3+NaOH→CHX3COONa+CHX3OH\ce{CH3COOCH3 + NaOH -> CH3COONa + CH3OH}CHX3​COOCHX3​+NaOH​CHX3​COONa+CHX3​OHSwipe to see the whole equation →

  6. Check: S = CHX3COOCHX3\ce{CH3COOCH3}CHX3​COOCHX3​ = CX3HX6OX2\ce{C3H6O2}CX3​HX6​OX2​ ✔. Every equation balances, e.g. step 2: C 4 | 4, H 8 | 6 + 2, O 4 | 4, Na 2 | 2 ✔.

  7. Answer C ethanoic acid, R sodium ethanoate, A methanol, S methyl ethanoate; four equations above.

    Common trap: Taking A as ethanol "because that is the usual alcohol". Ethanol would give a four-carbon ester, CX4HX8OX2\ce{C4H8O2}CX4​HX8​OX2​, not CX3HX6OX2\ce{C3H6O2}CX3​HX6​OX2​.

E12●●● AdvancedLong answer · 5 marksNCERT Exemplar Ch4 LA 57

An organic compound A on heating with concentrated HX2SOX4\ce{H2SO4}HX2​SOX4​ forms a compound B which on addition of one mole of hydrogen in presence of Ni forms a compound C. One mole of compound C on combustion forms two moles of COX2\ce{CO2}COX2​ and 3 moles of HX2O\ce{H2O}HX2​O. Identify the compounds A, B and C and write the chemical equations of the reactions involved.

Full solution

Given: A → B (conc. HX2SOX4\ce{H2SO4}HX2​SOX4​); B + HX2\ce{H2}HX2​ (Ni) → C; 1 C → 2 COX2\ce{CO2}COX2​ + 3 HX2O\ce{H2O}HX2​O. Asked: A, B, C; equations.

Concept used: work backwards from the combustion; addition; dehydration (Topics 6–7).

  1. 1

    2 COX2\ce{CO2}COX2​ → 2 C atoms; 3 HX2O\ce{H2O}HX2​O → 6 H atoms → C = CX2HX6\ce{C2H6}CX2​HX6​, ethane.

  2. 2

    C was made by adding one HX2\ce{H2}HX2​ to B → B = CX2HX4\ce{C2H4}CX2​HX4​, ethene.

  3. 3

    Ethene comes from heating an alcohol with concentrated sulphuric acid → A = ethanol.

    CHX3CHX2OH→hot conc.  HX2SOX4CHX2=CHX2+HX2O\ce{CH3CH2OH ->[\text{hot conc. } H2SO4] CH2=CH2 + H2O}CHX3​CHX2​OHhot conc.  HX2​SOX4​​CHX2​=CHX2​+HX2​OSwipe to see the whole equation →
    CHX2=CHX2+HX2→NiCHX3−CHX3\ce{CH2=CH2 + H2 ->[\text{Ni}] CH3-CH3}CHX2​=CHX2​+HX2​Ni​CHX3​−CHX3​Swipe to see the whole equation →
    2 CX2HX6+7 OX2→4 COX2+6 HX2O\ce{2C2H6 + 7O2 -> 4CO2 + 6H2O}2CX2​HX6​+7OX2​​4COX2​+6HX2​OSwipe to see the whole equation →

  4. Check: the last equation per mole of ethane gives 2 COX2\ce{CO2}COX2​ and 3 HX2O\ce{H2O}HX2​O, as stated ✔; it balances: C 4 | 4, H 12 | 12, O 14 | 8 + 6 ✔.

  5. Answer A ethanol, B ethene, C ethane; equations above.

    Common trap: Writing C as CX2HX4\ce{C2H4}CX2​HX4​. Two moles of COX2\ce{CO2}COX2​ and three of water need six H atoms.
